bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Hourly Rates to Annual Pay: The Basics

If you’re looking at a job offer or comparing pay rates, understanding how an hourly rate translates into annual salary is essential. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours, as set by the National Employment Standards. So, annual gross pay ≈ hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives you a figure before tax, Medicare, and super.

For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. For a 38-hour week, that’s $1,004.90 per week, or $52,254.80 per year. If you’re a casual employee, you’re entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base rate, making the casual minimum $33.05 per hour. That loading is added to the base rate before the annual conversion.

### Why 38 Hours and the Fortnight

We use 38 hours because it’s the standard full-time week under most awards and the Fair Work Act. If you work part-time or different hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. The fortnight is simply weekly pay multiplied by two. For instance, $1,004.90 per week becomes $2,009.80 per fortnight. Many employers pay fortnightly, so it’s a handy figure for budgeting.

## Monash Salary Rates and Enterprise Agreements

Monash University sets its pay through enterprise agreements, which often provide higher rates than the minimums in modern awards. The [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman list award rates, but Monash salary rates are negotiated separately. For example, academic staff at Monash have specific salary scales for continuing and fixed-term roles, and professional staff have their own classifications. These rates are published on the Monash enterprise agreements page and are updated regularly.

When comparing a job offer from Monash to an award-covered role, remember that enterprise agreement rates can include additional benefits or conditions. Always check the applicable agreement or the Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database for the correct minimums.

## Distinguishing Award Rates, National Minimum Wage, and Casual Loading

It’s important to know the difference between the National Minimum Wage, award rates, and enterprise agreement rates. The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor for all employees not covered by an award or agreement. Award rates are minimums set for specific industries and occupations, and they often include penalty rates, allowances, and overtime. Enterprise agreements can vary these but must not leave employees worse off overall.

Casual loading is an extra payment to compensate for lack of paid leave and other entitlements. Under most awards, the loading is 25% of the base hourly rate. When using our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool, you can tick a checkbox to add 25% casual loading on top of the base rate you enter. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading – the tool handles that for you.

## Superannuation: Paid on Top

Superannuation guarantee is currently 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. This means if your annual gross pay is $60,000, your employer contributes an additional $7,200 to your super fund, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is not deducted from your pay; it’s an extra cost for the employer. When estimating your total remuneration package, include super as a separate component.

## Tax and Medicare for 2026–27

Resident tax rates for 2026–27 are progressive: no tax on the first $18,200, then 15% up to $45,000, 30% up to $135,000, 37% up to $190,000, and 45% above that. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income, with reductions for low-income earners. Our calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of calculation. This is an estimate only – your actual tax may differ based on your circumstances, including HELP debts or the Medicare levy surcharge.

### Example: Converting a Monash Salary Rate

Suppose a Monash professional staff member earns $35.00 per hour (base rate) under the enterprise agreement. For a 38-hour week, that’s $1,330 per week, or $69,160 per year. Add 12% super ($8,299) for a total package of $77,459. After tax and Medicare (assuming no other deductions), the take-home pay would be approximately $53,000 per year. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a more detailed breakdown.

## Using the Timesheet and Other Tools

Our [timesheet](/) lets you enter your base hourly rate and toggle casual loading. It then calculates weekly, fortnightly, and annual figures, along with estimated tax and super. For award-specific rates, refer to the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page or the Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides. If you’re comparing job offers, also check the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which shows full-time adult ordinary time earnings at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026).

Remember, the annual figure from our calculator assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It’s a starting point for your financial planning.

## Final Thoughts on Monash Salary Rates

Monash salary rates are a good example of how enterprise agreements can provide better pay than the minimums. Whether you’re a current employee or considering a role, understanding the conversion from hourly to annual helps you evaluate offers and budget. Always verify rates against the official Monash enterprise agreement or the Fair Work Commission’s database. For general award rates, the Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides are your go-to resource.

Use our tools to run your own numbers, and remember that super and tax are separate considerations. With the right information, you can make informed decisions about your pay.
